scenes.tts: What if the neurons are made, but never arrive?
scenes.visual: Title card: The Nucleus Left Behind. A thick, smooth cortex beside a normal folded one.
scenes.narration: What if the neurons are made, but never arrive?

scenes.tts: In classic lissencephaly, the cortex is thick and nearly smooth, with about four crude layers.
scenes.visual: The smooth cortex in section: four crude layers. The normal cortex: six layers.
scenes.narration: In classic lissencephaly, the cortex is thick and nearly smooth, with about four crude layers.

scenes.tts: Yet in isolated lissencephaly, the head is usually near normal in size at birth.
scenes.visual: Volume equals area times thickness. A thin sheet with a large area, and a block four to five times as thick with a quarter to a fifth of the area, hold the same volume. Label: plausibility check only.
scenes.narration: Yet in isolated lissencephaly, the head is usually near normal in size at birth.

scenes.tts: Children with Miller-Dieker syndrome lack a piece of one chromosome seventeen, including L I S one.
scenes.caption: Children with Miller-Dieker syndrome lack a piece of one chromosome 17, including LIS1.
scenes.visual: Chromosome 17 with region 17p13.3 deleted on one copy. LIS1 is marked inside it.
scenes.narration: Children with Miller-Dieker syndrome lack a piece of one chromosome 17, including LIS1.

scenes.tts: Losing only one copy of L I S one still causes lissencephaly. Half a dose is too little.
scenes.caption: Losing only one copy of LIS1 still causes lissencephaly. Half a dose is too little.
scenes.visual: One normal copy, one broken copy. Label: haploinsufficiency, half a dose is too little.
scenes.narration: Losing only one copy of LIS1 still causes lissencephaly. Half a dose is too little.

scenes.tts: A mould gave the clue. Its relative of L I S one helps space nuclei, as do parts of dye-neen, a microtubule motor.
scenes.caption: A mould gave the clue. Its relative of LIS1 helps space nuclei, as do parts of dynein, a microtubule motor.
scenes.visual: A mould filament with evenly spaced nuclei; in the nudF mutant the nuclei bunch. Label: nudF, 42 percent identical to human LIS1.
scenes.narration: A mould gave the clue. Its relative of LIS1 helps space nuclei, as do parts of dynein, a microtubule motor.

scenes.tts: In mammalian cells, L I S one binds dye-neen and helps it work.
scenes.caption: In mammalian cells, LIS1 binds dynein and helps it work.
scenes.visual: Dynein walking along a microtubule toward its minus end. LIS1 bound to dynein, with NDE1 and NDEL1.
scenes.narration: In mammalian cells, LIS1 binds dynein and helps it work.

scenes.tts: A migrating neuron moves in two steps. First the leading process extends, and the centrosome moves into it. Then dye-neen pulls the nucleus up toward the centrosome.
scenes.caption: A migrating neuron moves in two steps. First the leading process extends, and the centrosome moves into it. Then dynein pulls the nucleus up toward the centrosome.
scenes.visual: A neuron on a radial glial fibre: stroke one, the leading process extends and the centrosome moves forward into it; stroke two, dynein on microtubules running back from the centrosome pulls the nucleus up toward it.
scenes.narration: A migrating neuron moves in two steps. First the leading process extends, and the centrosome moves into it. Then dynein pulls the nucleus up toward the centrosome.

scenes.tts: Predict. Knock down L I S one in the embryonic rat cortex. Does the process fail, the nucleus, or something earlier?
scenes.caption: Predict. Knock down LIS1 in the embryonic rat cortex. Does the process fail, the nucleus, or something earlier?
scenes.visual: Question card over the two strokes: which fails, the process, the nucleus, or something earlier?
scenes.narration: Predict. Knock down LIS1 in the embryonic rat cortex. Does the process fail, the nucleus, or something earlier?

scenes.tts: Most cells never started, and stayed many-branched. In the few that did, the process kept growing, but the nucleus stayed behind.
scenes.visual: Credit: Tsai and colleagues, 2005, embryonic rats. Most cells stay multipolar near the ventricle; one bipolar cell's process extends while its nucleus stays low.
scenes.narration: Most cells never started, and stayed many-branched. In the few that did, the process kept growing, but the nucleus stayed behind.

scenes.tts: The knockdown also blocked progenitor divisions at the ventricle. So L I S one has one foot in too few.
scenes.caption: The knockdown also blocked progenitor divisions at the ventricle. So LIS1 has one foot in too few.
scenes.visual: Inset: progenitor nuclei frozen in the ventricular zone. A two-column board: LIS1 sits in wrong place, overlapping into too few.
scenes.narration: The knockdown also blocked progenitor divisions at the ventricle. So LIS1 has one foot in too few.

scenes.tts: A second gene makes doublecortin. It is not a motor. It binds microtubules, and is thought mainly to steady the tracks.
scenes.visual: Doublecortin molecules along a microtubule. Label: DCX, on the X chromosome.
scenes.narration: A second gene makes doublecortin. It is not a motor. It binds microtubules, and is thought mainly to steady the tracks.

scenes.tts: Now the puzzle. A boy and his mother share a mutation that breaks doublecortin. He has a smooth brain; she has a second band.
scenes.visual: Two MRI-style outlines: his smooth, thick cortex; her nearly normal cortex with a band of gray matter beneath it.
scenes.narration: Now the puzzle. A boy and his mother share a mutation that breaks doublecortin. He has a smooth brain; she has a second band.

scenes.tts: The clue: a male has one X. Each of a female's cells silences one of her two X chromosomes at random.
scenes.visual: Male cell with one X. Female cells, each with one X greyed out at random. Label: X inactivation.
scenes.narration: The clue: a male has one X. Each of a female's cells silences one of her two X chromosomes at random.

scenes.tts: Predict. Explain both brains.
scenes.visual: Question card: explain both brains.
scenes.narration: Predict. Explain both brains.

scenes.tts: His one X carries the mutation, so no neuron makes working doublecortin. Most stall, and the cortex is smooth.
scenes.visual: Label: severe loss of function, in every cell. All his neurons tinted mutant; most stop low.
scenes.narration: His one X carries the mutation, so no neuron makes working doublecortin. Most stall, and the cortex is smooth.

scenes.tts: Her cortex is a mosaic. Neurons with the normal X active arrive. Those with the mutant X active stall partway, and gather into a band beneath the cortex.
scenes.visual: Her neurons tinted by active X: normal-X neurons climb to the cortex; mutant-X neurons stop and form a band beneath it.
scenes.narration: Her cortex is a mosaic. Neurons with the normal X active arrive. Those with the mutant X active stall partway, and gather into a band beneath the cortex.

scenes.tts: In embryonic rats, neurons with doublecortin silenced stalled, and formed such a band.
scenes.visual: Rat cortex section: silenced neurons form a band beneath the cortex.
scenes.narration: In embryonic rats, neurons with doublecortin silenced stalled, and formed such a band.

scenes.tts: Some neighbours were disturbed too, and the sorting has not been traced neuron by neuron in humans.
scenes.visual: Caveat card: some neighbours also disturbed; not yet shown neuron by neuron in human tissue.
scenes.narration: Some neighbours were disturbed too, and the sorting has not been traced neuron by neuron in humans.

scenes.tts: So read a cortex two ways. Size counts the doublings. Layering records the journey.
scenes.visual: Closing sorting board: size counts the doublings; layering records the journey.
scenes.narration: So read a cortex two ways. Size counts the doublings. Layering records the journey.
